scenes.name: The Rolling Stones
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Andrew Loog Oldham, su Svengali adolescente, los moldeó como los anti-Beatles: groseros y divisivos, «monstruos melenudos del Id adolescente» (tras la multa por orinar contra el muro de un garaje en 1965, puso a Jagger en el titular). En 1965 «(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction», con su fuzz y su racimo final de «no», expresó una insatisfacción casi cósmica con el consumismo que los había encumbrado; Jagger, culto y elocuente en Charlie Is My Darling de Peter Whitehead, decía que el pop por fin hablaba de levantarse, ir a trabajar y sentirse jodido. «19th Nervous Breakdown» (4 de febrero de 1966), grabado en Los Ángeles al final de una gira de cuarenta fechas, fue la primera gran declaración pop del año: dos guitarras metálicas entrelazadas (Richards y Brian Jones por última vez en un single), ritmo rockabilly maníaco, casi cuatro minutos sobre una pobre niña rica sin salida. Cada single debía superar al anterior en doce semanas. Mientras se codeaban con Anita Pallenberg, Robert Fraser o Christopher Gibbs, Aftermath (abril), entero de composiciones propias, fue el LP del año, aunque en «Stupid Girl» o «Under My Thumb» el desprecio por las mujeres no inquietó a nadie.

podcast.title: TV Out the Window (1972)
podcast.body: While staying in room 1015 at the Hyatt Continental on Sunset Boulevard in Hollywood, Keith Richards decided to throw his television out the window. This event is cited as the origin of the "rock and roll trope" of destroying hotel rooms by throwing a TV out the window. "Keith Richards, who was staying in room 1015, decided that he would throw his TV out the window."

podcast.title: Toronto Drug Bust (February 1977)
podcast.body: Keith Richards was busted for heroin and cocaine in February 1977 at what was then known as the Harbor Castle Hilton in Toronto. The exact room number was not specified in the account. "Keith Richards was busted for heroin and coke in February 1977."

podcast.title: Producer and Guitarist on Jumpin' Jack Flash (1986)
podcast.body: Keith Richards, guitarist for The Rolling Stones, produced and played guitar on Aretha Franklin's cover of "Jumpin' Jack Flash," the first single from her 1986 *Aretha* album. "special guest Keith Richards came in to produce and play guitar on the album's first single, a cover of the Rolling Stones classic Jumpin' Jack Flash"

podcast.title: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Inductor (1987)
podcast.body: Richards gave the induction speech for Aretha Franklin at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame ceremony in New York City on January 3, 1987, just months after collaborating on her "Jumpin' Jack Flash" cover. "Rolling Stones guitarist Keith Richards, who had helped Franklin score a hit with a cover of the Stones jump and jack flash just a few months earlier, gave the speech inducting her at the Waldorf Astoria in New York City."

podcast.body: Following Allan Klein's acquisition of the rights to The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony," he assigned songwriting credits to Keith Richards and Mick Jagger on all copies of the song and the album Urban Hymns, even though neither composed the sampled musical phrase. "who then slapped the names Jagger Richards on all the copies of the song and the album Urban Hymns."

podcast.title: Discomfort with Legal Process
podcast.body: Keith Richards, alongside Mick Jagger, publicly stated their lack of intention and disagreement with being involved in the complex legal battles surrounding "Bitter Sweet Symphony." Their declarations underscored a desire to not participate in what they viewed as an inappropriate legal entanglement. "Tato Mink Jaer como Chris Riches en el pasado han hecho varias declaraciones respecto a todo este proceso legal tan complejo del que se han visto en versos y ellos no tenían ninguna intención de ver si en estos rollos si no lo consideran correcto."

podcast.title: Grammy Nomination for "Bitter Sweet Symphony"
podcast.body: Keith Richards, along with Mick Jagger and Richard Ashcroft, was nominated for a Grammy for "Best Song of the Year" for "Bitter Sweet Symphony." This nomination was a result of the legal settlement that recognized them as composers, despite their actual role in the Verve's version being indirect through the sampled material. "el Grammy en mejor canción del año y en ese momento acabaron nominados que Dricha sin minchakers por una canción que ni siquiera habían compuesto."

podcast.title: Initial Reluctance on Fuzz for "Satisfaction"
podcast.body: When writing and recording "Satisfaction," Keith Richards used the Maestro Fuzz tone pedal to mimic a horn section for the iconic riff, intending it as a temporary placeholder. As a blues musician, he preferred a real horn section, but the rest of The Rolling Stones loved the guitar sound and overruled him. This decision led to the distorted guitar being permanently featured front and center in rock music. "Chief hated it. He was a blues guy. He wanted a horn section, but he was overruled in four weeks after the final session at RCA Studios in Hollywood on May 12, 1965."

podcast.title: Live Aid Performance
podcast.body: Keith Richards performed at Live Aid in Philadelphia on July 13, 1985, alongside Bob Dylan and Ron Wood of The Rolling Stones. Their collective performance was noted as arguably "one of the worst performances of his life" by Bob Dylan. "It was at Live Aid in Philadelphia on July 13 1985 that Bob Dylan who with Keith Richards and Ron Wood of the Rolling Stones arguably gave one of the worst performances of his life."

podcast.title: Masking Tape Songwriting Method
podcast.body: Keith Richards, while staying at the Sunset Marquis, once used masking tape with numbers to note the order of piano keys to remember a song he had written in his sleep, demonstrating a unique method for capturing musical ideas without formal theory knowledge or recording equipment. "He came to his room the next morning and he had taped, put a piece of masking tape down with numbers like the order that you play the notes in. That's so funny. Brilliant."

podcast.title: Melody Re-Writer for "The Last Time"
podcast.body: While "The Last Time" by The Rolling Stones was based on the gospel song "Dismay Vide Last Time," Keith Richards was responsible for re-writing its melody. This distinction is crucial in the complex authorship debate, as the gospel original provided much of the lyrical basis, but the melody itself was a new creation by Richards. "la canción de gospel había sido el inicio acreditado de la gran parte de la letra del last time perno de la melodía la cual fue rescritada porque Ritcha sin minchak."

xref.title: Seeking Treatment in England (2010)
xref.body: In November 2010, while in England, Courtney Love sought treatment for addiction, stating she needed "nurses and doctors." She reportedly reached out to Marlon Richards, son of Keith Richards, for help. "Need nurses and doctors, she wrote."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Keith Richards' 2023 View on Modern Music
xref.body: In 2023, Keith Richards expressed strong disapproval of modern music production techniques, citing the use of "push button drums" and synthesized sounds. He described digital recording as a "one-way toilet," indicating his preference for older, more organic methods of music creation. This sentiment from Richards, who played guitar for Mick Jagger on the song "Man, What a Drag It Is Getting Old," highlights a generational perspective on musical change. "Don't get me going on modern day music, push button drums and everything is synthesized. Digital recording is a one-way toilet."

xref.title: Copyright Dispute and Loss of Publishing Rights
xref.body: The Verve faced a significant legal battle over their song "Bittersweet Symphony," stemming from a licensed sample. Despite an initial agreement for 50% of earnings, Abkco Music (controlled by Allen Klein) and Andrew Loog Oldham sued, leading to The Verve being forced to surrender 100% of the song's publishing rights, resulting in Mick Jagger and Keith Richards being credited as co-writers and receiving all royalties. "Alright, give us 100% of the money made from this song or we will force you to recall every single copy of the song an album from every store and radio station and whatever worldwide."

"who then slapped the names Jagger Richards on all the copies of the song and the album Urban Hymns."

xref.title: Influence on British Rock Legends
xref.body: During her European tour in the spring of 1964, Sister Rosetta Tharpe performed in Manchester, where her inspiring performance deeply affected audience members Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck, Keith Richards, and Brian Jones of The Rolling Stones. These future rock icons became her "disciples" after witnessing her groundbreaking show. "Her performance was so inspiring that it changed the lives of four notable members of the audience."

xref.title: Pioneer of Electric Guitar Distortion
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharp was one of the very first musicians to intentionally use distortion on the electric guitar, a technique that would later become fundamental to rock music. Her innovative approach to the instrument had a significant impact on guitarists like Eric Clapton and Keith Richards. "There's more to she was one of the very first people to use distortion on the electric guitar."

xref.title: Profound Influence on Blues and Rock Pioneers
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe had a deep impact on the trajectory of the blues and on the pioneers of rock and roll, including major figures like Little Richard, Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Johnny Cash, all of whom were ardent fans. Her work also captivated British musicians such as Keith Richards, Eric Clapton, and Jeff Beck. "What is not in dispute is that sister Rosetta Tharp had a profound effect on the course of the blues, and then with the pioneers of rock."

xref.title: Trilobite Species after Keith Richards
xref.body: The same scientists, Adrian and Edgecomb, who found Mick Jagger's trilobite also discovered another species, which they named *parahedulous Richard's Eye*.
